Egg clusters of the Northwestern salamander, Ambystoma gracile, are typically deposited in still or slow-moving water, where each individual egg is encased in a distinct gelatinous capsule. Upon hatching at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the emerging yolk-sac larvae are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This extraordinarily low mass, which is derived from an egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters, underscores the lecithotrophic strategy of the earliest larval stage, during which the young rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The duration of this fully yolk-dependent period, from oviposition through the completion of hatching, is reported to be 49 days [ab = 49 days] when maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This developmental period is comparatively lengthy among pond-breeding ambystomatids, likely reflecting the cool, oligotrophic conditions of many montane nursery habitats where slower metabolic rates prolong embryonic development.

After the yolk-sac is fully resorbed, the free-swimming larva enters an extended period of active growth as an exogenously feeding tadpole. This aquatic larval stage, during which individuals exhibit conspicuous gill-breathing and a pronounced caudal fin, culminates in a major morphological transformation. The period from hatching to the onset of metamorphic climax, which involves the reabsorption of gills and tail fin and the development of limbs, spans approximately 395 days  under a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This remarkably long larval duration, exceeding a full year, is a hallmark of high-elevation populations and distinguishes A. gracile from many lowland congeners. Following this extended aquatic phase, the newly metamorphosed juvenile, sometimes called an eft, emerges onto land, though it may remain near the natal pond. The transformation is a critical life-stage transition that exposes the animal to a new suite of terrestrial predators and environmental stressors.

Following terrestrial recruitment, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult period before attaining sexual maturity. For females, puberty is achieved 730 days following metamorphosis [tp = 730 days following metamorphosis], when maintained at an average temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This represents a substantial delay, highlighting a life-history strategy that prioritizes achieving a large body size before initiating the costly process of gametogenesis. The maximum adult body mass attained by females, which reflects the asymptotic weight reached after this extended growth period, is 26.43 grams [Wwi = 26.43 grams]. This ultimate wet weight is relatively large compared to other salamanders of the genus, a trait that is likely linked to the high fecundity required to offset the risks of an unpredictable aquatic breeding environment. Gravid females carrying a complement of yolked ova thus represent a significant energetic investment accumulated over several years.

Reproductive output in this species is tied to the large body size achieved during the long juvenile phase. A gravid female produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and within that single annual event, she deposits between 150 and 200 eggs [Ri = annual event, she deposits between 150 and 200 eggs]. This pattern of iteroparity with a low annual frequency suggests that the energetic costs of vitellogenesis are substantial, requiring a full season of foraging to amass sufficient reserves for a single, large clutch. The accompanying metabolic demand of a reproductively active adult at rest has been measured at 0.0104 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0104 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animal is acclimated to 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This basal rate reflects the relatively low metabolic intensity typical of cool-adapted, high-latitude urodeles and provides a baseline for understanding the physiological costs associated with growth and reproduction.

The cumulative effect of this slow growth, late maturity, and low annual reproductive frequency is a life span that is exceptionally long for a temperate amphibian. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations are estimated to live up to 10.2 years [am = up to 10.2 years] under a mean annual temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This maximum longevity, which is among the highest recorded for any member of the Ambystomatidae, is consistent with a demographic strategy that spreads reproductive effort over many seasons. Natural mortality in the oldest age classes is typically attributed to senescence, as physiological functions gradually decline, and older individuals may become more susceptible to desiccation during dry years or to predation by larger vertebrates. The combination of a high age at first reproduction and a long reproductive life span means that even a low annual clutch frequency can result in a high lifetime fecundity, ensuring population persistence in the variable climate of the Pacific Northwest.
